sentences.text: This small pterosaur measured roughly one meter in length with a wingspan of approximately 100 centimeters.
Its flight was powered by a very large fourth finger that supported the wing membrane.
The animal possessed unique multi-cusped teeth, a feature that distinguishes it from almost all other pterosaurs which typically had simple or no teeth.
Despite its specialized teeth, it retained basal traits such as pterygoid teeth and a flexible tail lacking the rigid vertebral extensions found in other long-tailed pterosaurs.
Eudimorphodon held the record for the strongest dental occlusion known among pterosaurs, allowing its top and bottom teeth to touch directly when the jaws closed.
Fossil evidence of its diet includes preserved stomach contents containing fish of the genus Parapholidophorus.
The creature was featured in an episode of Animal Planet's Animal Armageddon, where it was described as a gull-like animal feeding on fish and carrion.
The genus was discovered in 1973 by Mario Pandolfi in Cene, Italy, and the type species, E. ranzii, was described by Rocco Zambelli the same year.
The specific name honors Professor Silvio Ranzi.
Additional fossil jaw fragments with multi-cusped teeth were found in 1986 in the Dockum Group rocks of western Texas.
Scientists have recorded 13 fossil occurrences of this genus to date.
The mouth featured four upper and two lower fangs per side followed by smaller multi-cusped teeth, with 25 upper and 26 lower teeth mostly having five cusps.
Evidence suggests the animal could crush or chew its food, as shown by the multi-cusped teeth and wear patterns.
Wear along the sides of the teeth indicates it likely fed on hard-shelled invertebrates in addition to fish.
The animal may have had a diamond-shaped structure at the end of its long bony tail, similar to later Rhamphorhynchus.
If present, this diamond-shaped tail structure may have acted as a rudder to help steer Eudimorphodon in the air.
Eudimorphodon is believed to be a member of the specialized off-branch Campylognathoididae, separate from the main lineage of pterosaur evolution.
Within this family, it is classified within the subfamily Eudimorphodontinae.
The genus includes the species E. ranzii described in 1973 and E. cromptonellus named in 2001.
A second species, E. rosenfeldi, was named by Dalla Vecchia in 1995 based on two specimens found in Italy.
Eudimorphodon lived during the Late Triassic, spanning from 219 to 215 million years ago, and is one of the oldest known pterosaurs.
Its range extended from the Norian to the Rhaetian stages, between 227.3 and 201.4 million years ago.
A 2020 study by Matthew G. Baron suggests Eudimorphodon groups with the clade Novialoidea within Lonchognatha, differing from the Campylognathoididae placement.
Due to a scarcity of primitive pterosaur remains, its evolutionary origins remain a mystery, with some experts suggesting affinities with dinosauriforms, arcosauriforms, or prolacertiforms.
